hierarchy-of-evidence.definition: A ranking of study types by how well they can show cause and effect: cell and animal studies at the bottom, randomised trials and reviews of trials near the top.

observational-study.definition: A study that watches what happens to people who chose, or were given, a treatment in daily life. Nobody decides by chance who gets what, so other differences between the groups can explain the result.

case-control-study.definition: A study that starts with people who have a disease (cases) and compares them with similar people who do not (controls), looking back at what they were exposed to.

systematic-review.definition: A review that searches for every study on a question with a method set in advance, judges each study's quality and sums up the whole body of evidence.

meta-analysis.definition: A calculation that combines the results of several studies into one overall estimate. It is only as good as the studies that go into it.

narrative-review.definition: A review in which the authors choose which studies to discuss, without a set search method. Useful as an overview, but open to the authors' own selection.

umbrella-review.definition: A review of systematic reviews: it collects many reviews on related questions and compares what they found.

control-group.definition: The group in a study that does not get the treatment being tested, or gets a placebo or another treatment. Without it you cannot tell what would have happened anyway.

randomisation.definition: Deciding by chance, like a coin toss, who gets the treatment and who does not. It tends to make the groups alike in everything except the treatment, including things nobody measured. The bigger the groups, the better this works.

allocation-concealment.definition: Keeping the next group assignment hidden from the researchers until a participant has joined, so they cannot steer particular people or animals into one group.

blinding.definition: Keeping participants, researchers or the people who measure the results from knowing who got the treatment. Expectations then cannot colour what is reported or measured.

sample-size.definition: The number of people or animals in a study, often written as n. A good study works out in advance how many it needs.

statistical-power.definition: The chance that a study finds an effect if the effect is real. Small studies have low power: they miss real effects, and the effects they do find are often too large.

false-positive.definition: A result that seems to show an effect when there is none, for example by chance in a small study.

pre-registration.definition: Publishing a study's plan, including its main outcome, in a public register before it starts. Later changes to the plan can then be seen.

selective-outcome-reporting.definition: Reporting the results that came out well and leaving out, or quietly changing, the ones that did not.

surrogate-endpoint.definition: A measurement that stands in for what really matters, such as a blood value instead of heart attacks. It is quicker to measure, but improving it does not always help the patient.

clinical-endpoint.definition: An outcome that matters to the patient directly: living longer, avoiding a heart attack, walking again, feeling better.

effect-size.definition: How big a difference a treatment makes, for example how many kilograms or how many fewer heart attacks. It is a different question from whether the difference could be chance.

p-value.definition: A number that says how surprising the data would be if the treatment had no effect at all and the study was done properly. A small p-value is called statistically significant. It does not say how big or how important an effect is.

relative-risk.definition: A comparison of risk between two groups as a ratio or a percentage: "20% fewer". It does not tell you how common the problem was to begin with.

absolute-risk.definition: How many people out of a group are affected, for example 8 in 100. The absolute difference between two groups is the number of people a treatment actually changes things for.

number-needed-to-treat.definition: How many people need a treatment for one of them to avoid one bad outcome over a given time. It is 100 divided by the absolute difference in percentage points.

natural-frequency.definition: A risk written as a count of people, such as "15 in 1,000", rather than as a percentage or a ratio. Most people find counts easier to understand.

confounding.definition: When a third factor affects both who gets a treatment and the outcome, so the treatment looks as if it caused something it did not. Healthier people choosing a pill is a common example.

preprint.definition: A research paper posted online before peer review. Anyone can read it early, but no outside expert has checked it yet.

spin.definition: Wording that makes a result look better than the data show, for example highlighting a side result when the main result was negative.

risk-of-bias.definition: A structured check of how a study was done (randomisation, blinding, missing data, reporting) to judge how likely its result is distorted.

grade-approach.definition: An international method for rating how much confidence a body of evidence deserves for one specific question, used by many guideline groups. Ratings run from high to very low.

animal-model.definition: An animal in which researchers create a condition, such as a cut tendon or a blocked artery, to stand in for a human disease. The model is never exactly the human disease.

inbred-strain.definition: Laboratory animals bred brother to sister for many generations, so they are almost genetically identical. That makes results tidy, and less like a varied human population.

translational-research.definition: The work of carrying a finding from cells or animals into tested treatments for people, and the study of how often that succeeds.

external-validity.definition: Whether a result found in one setting, such as young healthy rats, also holds in another, such as older patients with other illnesses.

internal-validity.definition: Whether a study's own result is trustworthy: whether the difference it found was caused by the treatment and not by bias or chance.

allometric-scaling.definition: Adjusting a dose between species of different sizes using body weight or body surface area. In drug development it is one step towards a cautious first test dose in people, not a way to find a dose that works.

first-in-human-trial.definition: The first time a new medicine is given to people, often to a few healthy volunteers (for some medicines, patients), one small step at a time, under close medical watch.

mabel.definition: The lowest amount expected to have any effect at all in people, estimated from laboratory and animal data, ideally including human cells. Some regulators ask for it when the first dose for people is chosen.

monoclonal-antibody.definition: A lab-made antibody designed to attach to one specific target in the body. Many modern medicines are monoclonal antibodies.

t-cell.definition: A type of white blood cell that directs and carries out immune responses.

superagonist.definition: A molecule that switches a receptor on more strongly than the body's own signal does. TGN1412 was designed as one for a switch on T cells.

cytokine-storm.definition: A sudden flood of immune signalling molecules that causes fever, low blood pressure and organ damage. It can be life-threatening.

post-marketing-surveillance.definition: The tracking of side effects after a medicine is on the market, when far more people use it than in the trials. It is how rare harms are found.

conflict-of-interest.definition: A situation in which a researcher, author or adviser could gain, for example money or reputation, from a particular result. It does not make the result false, but it calls for independent checks.

study-sponsor.definition: The organisation that pays for and is responsible for a study, such as a company, a university or a government funder.

ghost-writing.definition: When the real writer of a paper, often paid by a company, is not named as an author.

guest-authorship.definition: When someone is named as an author who did little or none of the work, often to lend the paper a respected name.

key-opinion-leader.definition: An expert whom companies pay to speak, advise or teach about a product or a field, because other people trust them.

predatory-journal.definition: A publication that charges authors to publish but skips real peer review and editing, so almost anything gets printed.

impact-factor.definition: A number that measures how often a journal's papers are cited on average. It says nothing about whether a single paper is right, and fake versions exist.

citation-laundering.definition: Our name for a claim gaining authority by being cited from paper to paper, often review to review, without new data, until a guess reads like a fact.
